newsitem.title: NEPAL: China pledges to provide $10 mln grant to Nepal.
newsitem.headline: China pledges to provide $10 mln grant to Nepal.

text.p: China pledged to provide Nepal $10 million in grants, under an agreement signed on Wednesday, to promote economic and technical cooperation with the tiny Himalayan kingdom, officials said.
The agreement was signed between Chinese Minister for Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi and Nepali Commerce Minister Fateh Singh Tharu.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin and Nepal's King Birendra were present at the signing ceremony.
No details on the agreement were given.
The agreement was signed to mark King Birendra's 25 years on the throne and promote technical and economic cooperation between the two countries, an official statement said.
Jiang arrived in Nepal on Wednesday for a two-day state visit at the end of a South Asian tour which took him to India and Pakistan.

"The purpose of my visit to Nepal is to enhance friendship, deepen understanding and broaden cooperation which, I believe, will be achieved through the concerted efforts of both sides," Jiang said in a written statement after landing in Kathmandu.
Jiang is the first Chinese president to visit the Himalayan kingdom in 12 years. He was a guest of honour at a banquet hosted by King Birendra on Wednesday night.

"China sincerely hopes to constantly enhance cooperation with South Asian countries for common development...and strive together into the coming 21st century for lasting peace and stability in this region and prosperity all over Asia," Jiang said at the banquet.
Jiang's visit has drawn keen attention in Nepal, which is sandwiched between China to the north and India to the south.

In the 12 months to mid-July 1995, Nepal exported $4.7 million worth of goods to China and imported $57.6 million worth. The $52.9 million trade shortfall was 21 percent greater than during the previous 12-month period.
Earlier on Wednesday, Jiang was quoted by Nepal's official news agency as urging Nepal to produce more marketable goods for export to Tibet as a means of trimming the trade imbalance.
Nepal has strived to balance ties with its giant neighbour.
Kathmandu recognises China's sovereignty over Tibet and bow's to Beijing's sensitivities over Taiwan.

Nepali Prime Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba met Jiang and assured him the Himalayan kingdom would not allow Tibetan exiles to organise anti-China activities from Nepal, Chinese officials said. "We have not seen any serious political activity (in Nepal) which is hostile to China," Shen Guofang, a spokesman for the Chinese foreign ministry, told reporters.
